newsitem.title: UK: Britain promises tough tactics on cowboy directors.
newsitem.headline: Britain promises tough tactics on cowboy directors.

text.p: The new Labour government said on Thursday it would be tough on so-called "cowboy" directors, who rip consumers off or indulge in bad business practice.

"War has been declared on the cowboy director," consumer affairs minister Nigel Griffiths told a press conference. "I want to spell out to cowboys that Labour is getting even tougher in the future," he added.
Over 1,000 company directors were banned for unfit conduct in the year ending March 31, 1997, according to figures released on Thursday by the Department of Trade and Industry.
A total of 1,040 disqualification orders against unfit directors were made in the year, up 43 percent from the previous period.
The commonest reported misconducts include failure to keep proper accounting records, failure to submit tax returns or pay over taxes and continuing trading when the company is insolvent.
Griffiths said the Insolvency Service, which investigates such cases, "will subject these directors to even greater scrutiny in the year ahead."
He said he would be willing to name offenders and publicise their actions "to deter others from following their example."
Average bans are around three to five years and Peter Joyce, head of the Insolvency Service, said six directors were convicted last year for returning to business under a ban.
"Where we learn of such a person acting we would prosecute," he said.
Griffiths said he wanted to look at ways to streamline the process by which cowboy directors are dealt with, adding that he wanted "very much the focus to be on consumers and creditors."
Joyce said that he was "optimistic" that full application of directives would "in fact see the whole process speeded up," with no need at this stage for extra resources.
"My message to people who are ripping off consumers is there is no place for you in British business," Griffiths said.
